questions.question: What do the conflict markers in a Git conflict look like and what do they mean?
questions.title: Understanding Git Conflict Markers
questions.direct_answer: Git writes three markers into a conflicted file: **`<<<<<<< HEAD`** starts your current branch's version, **`=======`** divides the two sides, and **`>>>>>>> branch-name`** ends the incoming branch's version. You resolve by editing the file to keep the right code and **deleting all three marker lines** before committing. Setting `merge.conflictstyle` to `diff3` adds a middle `|||||||` section showing the common ancestor.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate has actually resolved real conflicts and understands the markers are temporary text they must remove, not Git syntax
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Committing a file with markers still in it — in Java they become comments, so it compiles but ships broken/confusing code
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention diff3/zdiff3 conflict style to reveal the common ancestor, which shows what each side actually changed

sections.title: Markers Are Git's Split-Screen Inside Your File
sections.content:
When Git can't auto-merge because both branches changed the same lines, it stops and writes **conflict markers** directly into the file at each clash, rather than guessing.

`<<<<<<< HEAD` opens **your current branch's** version, `=======` is the divider, and `>>>>>>> branch-name` closes the **incoming branch's** version. It's a split-screen comparison embedded in the source: both versions stacked between markers, waiting for you to decide. The markers are **temporary scaffolding** — Git won't let the merge complete until you edit the file, choose the correct logic, and delete all three lines. They carry no special meaning to Git after insertion; you remove them by hand.

sections.title: The Three Markers at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|<<<<<<< HEAD|~Top section|your current branch|the 'ours' side|where the conflict starts
emerald|=======|~The divider|splits the two versions|nothing above or below it stays|just a separator
amber|>>>>>>> branch|~Bottom section|the incoming branch|the 'theirs' side|names the other branch
violet|diff3 / zdiff3|~Optional middle|||||||| common ancestor|shows the original|reveals what each side changed

sections.title: Conflict Markers in a Java Service
Wrong: resolve the logic but leave a marker behind
Right: keep both behaviors, remove every marker
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Committing the markers**: in Java they turn into comments, so it compiles but leaves junk in the codebase.
- **Blindly keeping one side**: you may delete a real bug fix or feature — the right answer often merges both.
- **Not testing after resolving**: marker-free and compiling does not mean logically correct.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`<<<<<<< HEAD`** = your branch; **`=======`** = divider; **`>>>>>>> branch`** = incoming branch.
- **You must delete all three markers** before the merge can complete.
- **Markers are plain text** with no meaning to Git after insertion.
- **Correct resolution often combines both sides**, not just one.
- **`diff3`/`zdiff3` style** adds the common ancestor to clarify each change.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: When Git can't automatically merge two branches because both changed the same lines, it inserts conflict markers right into your file. There are three of them. The first is seven left angle brackets followed by HEAD, and that marks where your current branch's version starts. Then there's a line of seven equals signs that acts as a divider. Below that is the incoming branch's version, and it ends with seven right angle brackets followed by the branch name. So you're basically seeing both versions stacked in the same file with these markers as boundaries. To resolve it, I open the file, read both sides to understand what each branch was doing, edit the code to keep the correct logic — which often means combining parts of both — and then delete all three marker lines. The mistake freshers make is forgetting to delete the markers. In Java they often turn into comments, so the code still compiles, but now you've got these weird angle-bracket lines sitting in production. After editing, I stage the file with git add and commit to finish the merge. One tip that really helps is setting the conflict style to diff3 or zdiff3 in your Git config. That adds a third section showing what the code looked like before either branch touched it, which makes it much easier to see what each side actually changed and how to combine them.

questions.question: What is the step-by-step process for resolving a Git merge conflict?
questions.title: How to Resolve a Git Merge Conflict
questions.direct_answer: Run **`git status`** to find conflicted files (shown as *both modified*), open each and edit out the markers to the correct code, **`git add`** each resolved file to mark it done, then **`git commit`** to finish the merge. The trap: `git add` is what marks a conflict resolved — skip it and `commit` fails. **`git merge --abort`** cleanly cancels the whole thing.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate has the edit -> add -> commit workflow as muscle memory and knows the abort escape hatch
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Editing the file but forgetting git add, so commit still reports unresolved conflicts and the merge stays pending
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention git merge --abort to back out cleanly, and that you re-run the build/tests before completing the merge

sections.title: From Detection to a Finished Merge
sections.content: When a merge hits conflicts, Git pauses in a special **merge state** and marks the affected files. You stay there until every conflict is resolved and you tell Git you're done. The flow is always the same: **detect** the conflicted files, **edit** each to the correct code, **stage** them to mark resolution, and **commit** to finish. The key idea is that staging (`git add`) is Git's signal that a file is resolved — only once all conflicts are staged will `commit` complete the merge. If things look too hairy, **`git merge --abort`** returns you to the exact pre-merge state with nothing half-applied.

sections.title: Resolution Flow at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|Detect|~Find conflicts|git status|shows 'both modified'|under unmerged paths
amber|Edit|~Fix the code|open each file|keep correct logic|delete all markers
emerald|Stage|~Mark resolved|git add <file>|the mandatory step|tells Git it's done
violet|Finish|~Complete merge|git commit|creates merge commit|or git merge --abort to bail

sections.title: The Resolution Steps
sections.content:
| Step | Command | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Detect | `git status` | lists conflicted files as *both modified* |
| 2. Edit | open each file | keep correct code, delete all markers |
| 3. Stage | `git add <file>` | marks that file's conflict resolved |
| 4. Verify | `mvn test` | confirm the merge is logically correct |
| 5. Finish | `git commit` | creates the merge commit, exits merge state |
| Escape | `git merge --abort` | cancel cleanly, back to pre-merge state |

sections.title: The Full Workflow in the Terminal
sections.content:
```bash
# 1. Merge triggers a conflict
git merge feature/add-payment
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in OrderService.java

# 2. See what's conflicted
git status
#   both modified:   src/main/java/com/example/OrderService.java

# 3. Edit the file to resolve, then stage it
git add src/main/java/com/example/OrderService.java

# 4. Verify before finishing
mvn test

# 5. Complete the merge
git commit -m "merge: integrate feature/add-payment"

# Or, if it's too complex right now, back out cleanly:
git merge --abort
```

sections.title: Trap: edit, then commit without staging
sections.content:
```bash
# Edited the file to remove markers, but skipped git add
git commit -m "resolve conflict"
# error: Committing is not possible because you have unmerged files.
# fatal: Exiting because of an unresolved conflict.
# The merge is stuck in a pending state
```

sections.title: Fix: stage to mark resolved, then commit
sections.content:
```bash
git add src/main/java/com/example/OrderService.java   # marks it resolved
git status   # nothing under 'Unmerged paths' now
git commit -m "merge: integrate feature/add-payment"
# Merge completes; a two-parent merge commit is created
```
*`git add` is the only way to tell Git a conflict is handled — editing the file alone isn't enough.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting `git add`**: the most common error — the file is edited but unstaged, so `commit` refuses.
- **Trying to push before committing**: the merge isn't finished until you commit; pushing fails first.
- **Not building/testing after resolving**: hand-merged code can compile yet be logically wrong — run the tests.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`git status`** reveals conflicted files as *both modified*.
- **Edit** each file: keep the right code, remove every marker.
- **`git add`** marks a file resolved — this step is mandatory.
- **`git commit`** finishes the merge and creates the merge commit.
- **`git merge --abort`** cancels cleanly back to the pre-merge state.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: The first thing I do when Git reports a conflict is run git status to see exactly which files are conflicted. They show up under a section called unmerged paths with a both-modified label. Then I open each file, find the conflict markers, read both versions to understand what each branch was doing, and edit the file to keep the correct logic and remove all the markers. Here's the step freshers trip on: after editing, you have to run git add on that file. That's how you tell Git the conflict is resolved. If you skip it and try to commit, Git complains that there are still unmerged files, and the merge just sits there pending. Once I've staged all the conflicted files, I like to run the build and tests, because resolving the markers makes it compile but doesn't guarantee the logic is right. Then I run git commit to finish the merge, which creates a merge commit with two parents. The other thing worth knowing is git merge abort. If I open the conflicts and realize they're way more tangled than I expected, or I need to check with a teammate first, I can run git merge abort and it cleanly cancels everything, putting my working directory back exactly how it was before I started, with no half-merged mess.

questions.question: What is git mergetool and how do IDE tools help with conflict resolution?
questions.title: Using git mergetool and IDEs for Conflict Resolution
questions.direct_answer: **`git mergetool`** launches a configured visual diff app (kdiff3, meld, P4Merge) that shows a **three-way view** — your version (local), theirs (remote), and the common ancestor (base) — plus a merged-result pane. IDEs like **IntelliJ IDEA** and **VS Code** have the same three-way merge editor built in, with syntax highlighting. The base pane is the key: it shows what each side changed from the original.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows professional tooling exists and understands the value of the three-way (base) view over plain text markers
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Clicking Accept Yours/Theirs reflexively without reading both sides, discarding work the other branch added
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name tools you've used (IntelliJ's three-pane merge, VS Code's merge editor) and explain why the base pane is the most useful part

sections.title: Visual Three-Way Merging Beats Editing Markers by Hand
sections.content:
You *can* resolve conflicts by editing markers in a text file, but **visual merge tools** make it faster and safer. **`git mergetool`** launches an external app configured in your Git settings — kdiff3, meld, P4Merge, Beyond Compare.

These show a **three-way view**: your branch (local), the incoming branch (remote), and crucially the **common ancestor** (base) — what the code looked like before either side changed it. Seeing the base reveals what each side actually changed, which is the secret to combining them correctly. Modern IDEs — **IntelliJ IDEA**, **VS Code**, **Eclipse** — build the same three-way editor in, adding syntax highlighting, code navigation, and the ability to run tests right after resolving. Instead of hand-deleting markers (and risking leftovers), you click to accept sections and the tool guarantees clean output.

sections.title: The Three-Way View
sections.content:
blue|Local (yours)|~Left pane|your current branch|the 'ours' side|what you changed
amber|Remote (theirs)|~Right pane|the incoming branch|the 'theirs' side|what they changed
emerald|Base (ancestor)|~Middle pane|common starting point|the original code|reveals each side's diff
violet|Merged result|~Bottom pane|your final answer|click to accept sections|tool removes markers for you

sections.title: Configuring and Launching git mergetool
sections.content:
```bash
# Configure your preferred tool once (global)
git config --global merge.tool kdiff3

# On a conflict, launch the visual three-way view
git merge feature/refactor-payment
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in PaymentService.java
git mergetool
# Opens: LOCAL | BASE | REMOTE, with a MERGED result pane
# After you save, the tool stages the resolved file automatically

# Finish the merge
git commit -m "merge: refactor-payment (resolved via mergetool)"
```
*In IntelliJ, just open the conflicted file and click "Resolve" to get the same three-pane editor — no config needed.*

sections.title: Wrong: blindly accept one side in the tool
sections.content:
```bash
# In the merge UI, clicking 'Accept Theirs' on every chunk
# without reading the base or your own changes...
# -> silently drops the null-check your branch added
# The tool made it easy to discard real work
```

sections.title: Right: read all three panes, then combine
sections.content:
```bash
# Use the BASE pane to see what each side changed from the original,
# then build the MERGED pane to include BOTH:
#   - your branch's null-check
#   - their branch's refactored signature
# Save -> tool stages the file -> run tests -> commit
mvn test
git commit -m "merge: combine null-check with refactored signature"
```
*The base/ancestor pane is what turns 'pick a side' into 'understand both and merge correctly.'*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Reflexively accepting one side**: the Accept buttons are for trivial conflicts, not a substitute for reading both changes.
- **Never configuring a tool**: without `merge.tool` set, `git mergetool` may drop you into vimdiff — set it up once.
- **Ignoring the base pane**: the common-ancestor view is the most valuable part; without it you're guessing.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`git mergetool`** opens a configured visual three-way diff.
- **Three-way view** = local, remote, and base (common ancestor).
- **The base pane** shows what each side changed — the key to merging.
- **IDEs (IntelliJ, VS Code)** have the same editor built in, with highlighting.
- **Tools auto-remove markers and often auto-stage** the resolved file.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: git mergetool is a command that opens a visual diff program to resolve conflicts graphically instead of editing markers by hand. You configure which tool to use once in your Git config — popular free ones are kdiff3 and meld. When you run it during a conflict, it opens a window showing three versions of the code side by side. The left pane is your branch, the right pane is the incoming branch, and the middle pane is the base version — what the code looked like before either branch touched it. That middle pane is the most useful part, because it shows you what each side actually changed from the original, which makes it obvious how to combine them. At the bottom there's a merged pane where you build the final result, and the tool has buttons to accept sections from either side. Modern IDEs like IntelliJ have this built in — when you open a conflicted file, it shows the same three-way view with syntax highlighting, and I can run the tests immediately after resolving without leaving the editor. The big advantage over editing markers manually is that you see all three versions in context, so you don't accidentally throw away one side. Freshers sometimes just click accept theirs on everything, but if my branch added a null check and theirs refactored the method, accepting theirs blindly would silently drop my null check. Reading all three panes and combining is the whole point.

questions.question: How can you prevent or minimize merge conflicts in a team setting?
questions.title: Preventing Merge Conflicts
questions.direct_answer: Cut conflicts by keeping **feature branches short-lived** (merge within a few days), **pulling from `main` frequently** to stay synced, **communicating** before touching shared classes, and designing **modular code** so features live in different files. Most conflicts are a symptom of long-lived branches and a few god classes — fix the root cause, not just your resolution speed.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate thinks proactively about workflow and architecture, not just reactively resolving conflicts
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating conflicts as unavoidable and ignoring how branch lifetime and code structure drive their frequency
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect conflict frequency to architecture — modular packages, microservices, feature flags, trunk-based development shrink the overlap surface

sections.title: Conflicts Are a Symptom — Treat the Cause
sections.content:
Conflicts are unavoidable in parallel work, but their frequency depends on **team practice** and **code architecture**, not luck. The aim isn't zero conflicts; it's fewer and simpler ones.

**Short-lived branches** are the single biggest lever: a branch that merges in 1–3 days barely diverges from `main`, while a month-old branch is a conflict magnet. **Frequent integration** (pulling `main` daily) keeps you in sync incrementally instead of all at once. **Communication** stops two people from refactoring the same class in opposite directions. And **modular architecture** — features in separate packages/services — means parallel work rarely touches the same file. Think of conflicts as feedback about your process and design.

sections.title: Four Levers to Reduce Conflicts
sections.content:
amber|Short-lived branches|~Merge in 1-3 days|less divergence|feature flags hide WIP|trunk-based is the extreme
blue|Frequent pulls|~Stay synced|pull main daily|small conflicts early|not one giant one later
emerald|Communication|~Avoid overlap|flag shared refactors|standup / quick message|Git can't merge intentions
violet|Modular design|~Separate files|one feature per service|clear ownership zones|fewer shared hotspots

sections.title: Modular Design vs a God Class
Conflict-prone habit: long-lived branch, no syncing
sections.content:
```bash
# Branch once, vanish for three weeks, never pull main
git switch -c feature/big-thing
# ...20 commits while main moves on heavily...
git merge main   # huge conflicts across many files
```

sections.title: Conflict-resistant habit: short branch, daily sync
sections.content:
```bash
# Start each day in sync with the team
git switch main && git pull origin main
git switch feature/small-slice
git merge main           # tiny, easy conflicts (or none)
# Merge the slice back within a day or two via PR
```
*Pulling main daily turns one painful three-week conflict into a series of trivial one-day ones.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Accepting conflicts as fate**: most come from long-lived branches or god classes — fixable with habits and design.
- **Not pulling before new work**: building on stale `main` guarantees worse conflicts at merge time.
- **Relying on Git over talking**: Git merges code, not intentions — a 30-second message prevents hours of cleanup.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Short-lived branches** (1–3 days) dramatically reduce conflict accumulation.
- **Pull `main` daily** to integrate incrementally.
- **Communicate** before refactoring shared classes.
- **Modular architecture** keeps features in different files.
- **Feature flags / trunk-based development** let branches stay short even for big features.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: The biggest lever is keeping feature branches short-lived. If I merge my branch back to main every day or two, I just don't accumulate many conflicts, because main hasn't changed much since I branched. Long-lived branches that sit for weeks are conflict magnets — by the time you merge, main has diverged completely and you're fixing conflicts across dozens of files. The second habit is pulling from main frequently. I usually pull at the start of each day before I write any code, so I'm always working on top of the latest team changes, and any conflict is just from the last day, not the last month. A small conflict resolved early is far easier than a giant one later. Communication matters too. If I'm about to refactor a controller that I know another feature touches, I'll say so in standup or drop a quick message, because a lot of conflicts happen when two people don't realize they're working in the same place — and Git can merge code but it can't merge conflicting intentions. On the architecture side, good modular design naturally prevents conflicts. If payment logic lives in PaymentService and notifications live in NotificationService in separate files, two people can work in parallel without ever touching the same code. Compare that to one giant OrderService where every feature adds methods — that file becomes a permanent hotspot. Teams using microservices, or even just well-organized packages, see far fewer conflicts because the code boundaries match the team boundaries.

questions.question: How do rebase conflicts differ from merge conflicts?
questions.title: Rebase Conflicts vs Merge Conflicts
questions.direct_answer: A **merge** resolves conflicts **once** — it combines all changes in one three-way comparison and you finish with `git commit`. A **rebase** replays your commits one by one, so conflicts can appear **per commit** (you may fix the same file repeatedly), and you continue with **`git rebase --continue`**, not `git commit`. Rebase keeps history linear; `--abort` backs out, `--skip` drops a redundant commit.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands rebase replays commit-by-commit vs merge's single three-way combine, and the different completion commands
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Running git commit after resolving a rebase conflict instead of git rebase --continue, breaking the rebase sequence
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention git rebase --skip for commits superseded by the base and git rebase --abort to restore the original branch safely

sections.title: Once vs Commit-by-Commit
sections.content: Both merge and rebase produce conflicts when two branches touch the same lines, but they handle them very differently. A **merge** does a single three-way comparison — common ancestor, your tip, target tip — surfaces all conflicts together, and you finish with one **merge commit**. A **rebase** replays each of your commits one at a time onto the new base, so a conflict can appear on **each commit**, and you might resolve the **same file multiple times**. After each fix you run **`git rebase --continue`** (not `git commit`), and the result is a **linear history** with no merge commit. Picture merge as zipping two timelines at once, and rebase as replaying your commits step-by-step onto a new foundation.

sections.title: Rebase Conflicts vs Merge Conflicts
sections.content:
| Aspect | Merge | Rebase |
|---|---|---|
| **When conflicts appear** | once, all at once | per commit replayed |
| **Resolve same file** | once | possibly multiple times |
| **Continue command** | `git commit` | `git rebase --continue` |
| **Resulting history** | merge commit (graph) | linear, no merge commit |
| **Skip a commit** | n/a | `git rebase --skip` |
| **Back out** | `git merge --abort` | `git rebase --abort` |

sections.title: Merge vs Rebase Conflicts at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|Merge|~Resolve once|one three-way combine|finish with git commit|creates a merge commit
amber|Rebase|~Per commit|replays one at a time|finish with rebase --continue|stays linear
blue|Repeats|~Same file again|different commits overlap|fix it multiple times|normal, not a failure
rose|Escapes|~When stuck|rebase --skip (redundant)|rebase --abort (restore)|merge --abort for merges

sections.title: Trap: git commit during a rebase
sections.content:
```bash
git rebase main
# CONFLICT in OrderService.java (first replayed commit)
# fix the file...
git add OrderService.java
git commit -m "fixed"      # WRONG during a rebase
# Creates a stray commit and breaks the replay sequence
```

sections.title: Right: continue the replay
sections.content:
```bash
git rebase main
# CONFLICT in OrderService.java (commit 1 of 2)
git add OrderService.java
git rebase --continue       # move to the next replayed commit

# Same file may conflict again on commit 2:
git add OrderService.java
git rebase --continue

# Other escape hatches:
git rebase --skip           # drop a commit already in the base
git rebase --abort          # restore the original branch state
```
*During a rebase, `--continue` advances the replay; `git commit` is for merges, not rebases.*

sections.title: When Each Comes Up
sections.content: You hit **merge** conflicts on shared branches (`main`, `develop`) where you preserve history and resolve once — safer for teams. You hit **rebase** conflicts when tidying a private feature branch before a PR: accept that you may resolve a file across several commits in exchange for a clean, linear, reviewable history. A typical Java flow: rebase `feature/user-auth` onto the latest `main` before opening the PR, then merge the PR into `main`. If a rebase gets messy, `git rebase --abort` restores everything so you can fall back to a merge.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **`git commit` mid-rebase**: muscle memory from merging breaks the sequence — use `git rebase --continue`.
- **`--continue` without staging**: you must `git add` the resolved file first, or continue fails.
- **Rebasing shared commits**: rewriting commits teammates pulled causes divergence — rebase private branches only.
- **Panicking and force-pushing**: instead, `git rebase --abort` cleanly returns to the pre-rebase state.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Merge** = resolve once, finish with `git commit`, creates a merge commit.
- **Rebase** = resolve per replayed commit, continue with `git rebase --continue`.
- **Same file may conflict multiple times** during a rebase.
- **`git rebase --skip`** drops a commit already present in the base.
- **`git rebase --abort`** safely restores the original branch.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: The key difference is that merge conflicts happen all at once while rebase conflicts happen one commit at a time. When you merge, Git compares three snapshots — the common ancestor, your branch, and the target — and shows you all the conflicts together. You fix them, run git add, then git commit to create a merge commit that joins the two histories. With rebase, Git takes each of your commits and replays them one by one onto the target. So if you have three commits and two of them conflict, you resolve conflicts twice, and you might even fix the same file more than once if different commits touch overlapping lines. After each fix you run git add and then git rebase continue — not git commit. That's the command freshers get wrong most, because merge taught them to type git commit, and doing that mid-rebase breaks the sequence and creates a stray commit. If a commit turns out to be redundant because the base already has those changes, you can run git rebase skip to drop it. And if it gets too messy, git rebase abort cleanly exits and restores your branch to exactly where it was before. In a Java project you'd usually rebase your feature branch onto main before opening a PR to get a clean linear history, then merge the PR into main. The trade-off is cleaner history in exchange for more resolution steps.
